title: Evenings with Graham & Emmy
teaser: El-Sayed hits Saline data center on grid strain and water use—what it means for bills and towns.

lines.text: Good evening, and welcome to Evenings with Graham & Emmy — the Michigan Data Wire, your podcast on Michigan's data center buildout. I'm Graham.
And I'm Emmy.

Tonight we're talking about Democratic Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed taking direct aim at the Oracle-OpenAI data center planned for Saline, and what that means for power bills, water supplies, and local taxpayers across the state.

Graham, El-Sayed went on C-SPAN today and called out the project's expected draw on the electric grid and local water. He said the tax breaks and infrastructure strain would hit Michigan residents while the benefits go elsewhere.
That's right. This is the big hyperscale project that has already sparked local pushback in Washtenaw County over land use and now these bigger resource questions.
Why does this matter so much right now? Michigan has seen a wave of these proposals, right?

Exactly. Data centers have been landing in rural and suburban spots from Cass County to Macomb, and the pattern is the same: big power needs, cooling water demands, and fights over who pays for upgrades.
Walk me through the power side. What kind of load are we talking about with a project like this?

These facilities can pull hundreds of megawatts, sometimes approaching a gigawatt at full build. That's enough to power tens of thousands of homes, and utilities have to plan new lines or substations that eventually show up on everyone's bill.
And the water angle? El-Sayed flagged that too.

Cooling these servers takes a lot of water. Today we also saw the backers file for a permit to release treated wastewater into the river near Saline. Downstream residents are already asking what that means for quality and flow.
So the environmental price tag is becoming concrete. How does this tie into the tax breaks he mentioned?

The project is seeking incentives that could shift some infrastructure costs to local taxpayers while the company gets long-term abatements. El-Sayed argued that leaves residents holding the bag on higher rates and strained systems.
This sharpens the debate ahead of the August primary, as the story noted. What do you think voters in those areas are weighing?
Jobs and tax revenue versus reliability of power and water, plus long-term land use. It's the same tension playing out in St. Joseph County and Cass County where candidates are pushing moratoriums.
We saw a council hopeful today calling for a pause until rural impacts are clearer. How common is that stance now?
It's spreading. Yesterday Cass County residents organized to push zoning changes before more projects arrive, and a St. Joseph candidate is calling for a temporary halt over power and water spikes.
On the funding side, executives tied to the Saline project donated to Congresswoman Haley Stevens. Does that raise local influence questions in Washtenaw County?
It does for some residents. The donations link the same players pushing the project to a key federal voice, which could shape how incentives or oversight play out.
Meanwhile, a judge ruled today in the Shelby annexation fight. What does that mean for local control?
The decision clarifies whether the site can bypass county oversight. Macomb County residents now have clearer rules on approvals and potential tax revenue sharing going forward.
And in another twist, a hyperscale company sold Bitcoin to fund its Michigan AI campus. How does that financing angle affect things?
It shows crypto holdings are now directly bankrolling construction. Residents near that site will see new power lines and the same tax questions tied to the project.
Graham, stepping back, what's the bigger history here? Michigan has had these fights before.

Yes, earlier waves of proposals hit farmland preservation and quiet roads in places like Dowagiac. Yesterday U.S. Rep. Tim Walberg flagged potential robotics job risks tied to that project, weighing automation against local employment gains.
So the stakes are jobs versus automation concerns too. What happens next on the Saline front?
The August public session will lay out power use, jobs, and tax details for residents near the site. That's a direct chance to ask questions before permits advance.
And the water discharge permit is now in the mix. How might that play out?
State review will look at quality and downstream effects. If approved, it sets a precedent for other projects; if denied or conditioned, it could slow timelines.
El-Sayed's comments are landing right as the primary heats up. Any sense of how this resonates beyond Washtenaw?
Statewide, it highlights the tension between attracting tech investment and protecting ratepayers and resources. Other counties watching the Shelby and Cass fights will take notes.
What about the broader grid? Are utilities signaling they need more time or investment?
The August session is meant to address exactly that—projected demand and who covers upgrades. Residents will hear specifics on how it could affect their bills.
I keep coming back to the water permit filing today. That feels like a concrete next step.
It is. It puts an environmental price tag on the project that had mostly been discussed in abstract power and land terms until now.
And the tax break angle—how long could those incentives last?
Proposals often run 10-12 years or more. That stretches the period where local services might see strain without full revenue.
Graham, for listeners who live downstream or near the proposed lines, what practical questions should they bring to the August session?
Ask about peak demand timing, backup power plans, water recycling rates, and exactly how any tax abatements are structured. Those details determine real impacts.
This feels like it could set the tone for the rest of the summer. Any other counties moving on rules right now?
The St. Joseph and Cass pushes from yesterday show the momentum for local limits before more proposals land. Shelby's court ruling adds clarity on annexation paths.
All right, let's shift to quick hits. First up, that August data center session—residents get to hear power, jobs, and tax details directly.
Yes, it's a chance for neighbors to ask about local impacts before decisions move forward.
Next, a council hopeful wants a power-grid pause to block server farms until rural effects are known. Voters will decide if that protects resources or slows growth.
That stance could shape the race and future zoning battles in the county.
Tech giants filed today to dump treated water from the Saline facility into the river. Downstream residents could see quality and flow changes if approved.
It adds a specific environmental dimension to the scrutiny already on power and land.
Executives tied to the Saline project donated to Haley Stevens' campaign. Questions about influence in Washtenaw County are rising.
The link between project backers and federal representation is now part of the local conversation.
Court ruled today in the Shelby data center annexation fight. Macomb residents have clearer rules on approvals and tax revenue.
The outcome affects how future projects navigate county oversight.
Hyperscale sold Bitcoin to fund its Michigan AI campus. New power lines and tax questions are coming with construction.
Crypto financing is now directly tied to local buildouts.
Yesterday Cass County residents organized to shape future data center rules, aiming to protect farmland after the Dowagiac project.
County decisions will set how much industrial load the area accepts.
Also yesterday, Rep. Tim Walberg flagged robotics job risks tied to the Dowagiac data center. Residents are weighing gains against automation concerns.
Cass County voters will track training needs as the project advances.
And a St. Joseph County candidate is pushing a moratorium to block data centers over sudden power and water spikes.
Other counties are watching as they scramble to write their own limits.
On deck, the big August public session on the proposed data center will give residents a direct look at power, jobs, and tax effects.
Check your local notices for time and location—it's the place to get answers before anything advances.
Listeners in Macomb and Cass should also watch for any follow-up zoning or council meetings tied to the recent rulings and organizing efforts.
Full sources and the live map at the Michigan Data Center Tracker. We're back tomorrow.

episode_title: El-Sayed Slams Saline Oracle Project Over Power and Water Costs as Residents Brace for Imp
